sources.name: van den Hoek et al. (2024), Normative data for the squat, bench press and deadlift exercises in powerlifting: Data from 809,986 competition entries. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 27(10):734-742
sources.measures: Best successful competition bench press divided by the lifter's bodyweight at that competition (ratio), from drug-tested, unequipped (raw) powerlifting meets in 15 federations worldwide, 1968-2022, lifters aged 12+; athletes can appear more than once. Deciles for males aged 18-35 (UN young adult band), N = 306,061 bench press entries. Also stratified by IPF weight class (Table 6) and by other age bands (Table 4).
sources.unit_as_published: multiple of bodyweight (kg lifted / kg bodyweight)
sources.notes: Mean and SD are for all 571,650 male entries (all ages), not just 18-35; male mean bodyweight 88.3 kg (SD 20.0). Paper publishes only the 10th to 90th deciles; no 95th or 99th percentile and no absolute-kg bench values in the main text (absolute totals are in supplementary Tables S4-S5, not the bench press alone). Other male age bands, p50/p90: 12-17 1.24/1.63 (N 69,494); 36-59 1.51/1.92 (N 111,152); 60-79 1.23/1.60 (N 22,289); 80+ 0.93/1.31 (N 789). Weight-class p90 bench ratios: 74 kg 2.00, 83 kg 1.96, 93 kg 1.89, 105 kg 1.82, 120 kg 1.75. Open access (CC BY 4.0); full text read from the UniSC repository copy.

sources.name: Strength Level, Bench Press Standards for Men and Women (kg)
sources.measures: Estimated one-rep-max bench press from sets logged by Strength Level app/site users (self-reported gym lifts, not competition), converted to an estimated 1RM; standards built from regression on the community data, with unrealistic lifts and automated entries excluded. Levels are defined as percentiles: Beginner = stronger than 5% of lifters, Novice 20%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 80%, Elite 95%. Values below are the male overall (all bodyweights) standards; the page also tabulates by bodyweight and by age.
sources.notes: n is the number of qualifying male results (9,906,475 of 10,923,537 qualifying results drawn from 48,718,584 community lifts, data 22 March 2015 to 10 March 2026); it counts lifts, not unique lifters. No 99th percentile is published. By age the male Elite (p95) value is 156 kg at 20, 160 kg at 25-40, 142 kg at 50, 120 kg at 60. By bodyweight the male Elite value is 136 kg at 70 kg, 151 kg at 80 kg, 165 kg at 90 kg, 179 kg at 100 kg. Self-selected, self-reported sample of people who log workouts; not the general population.

sources.name: Fitness Volt, Bench Press Standards by Bodyweight (competition percentiles by weight class)
sources.measures: Percentiles of best raw (unequipped) competition bench press for male lifters, computed by Fitness Volt from the OpenPowerlifting open dataset, segmented by bodyweight class. Tested and untested meets pooled; no year range stated. Values below are the 83 kg class (largest single class, n = 96,625 results).
sources.unit_as_published: lb with kg equivalents (kg shown here)
sources.notes: Only source found that publishes a 99th percentile, but only per weight class, never for all men combined. p99 in kg by class: 59 kg 162.5; 66 kg 160.5; 74 kg 172.5; 83 kg 187.5; 93 kg 200.0; 105 kg 215.0; 120 kg 230.0; 120+ not listed (125 kg class 250.0; 140 kg class 270.0). p50 by class: 74 kg 112.5; 93 kg 132.5; 105 kg 145.0; 120 kg 155.0. Not independent of van den Hoek 2024 (same underlying OpenPowerlifting records, but with different filters: Fitness Volt does not restrict to drug-tested federations). Commercial site; year is the access year, the page states no data cutoff.

sources.name: Strength Origins, Bench Press Standards (2025 competition percentiles)
sources.measures: Best competition bench press for male lifters in raw, drug-tested, full-power (squat-bench-deadlift) sanctioned meets held 1 Jan to 20 Dec 2025, ages 16-65, one best result per lifter per year; percentiles computed by Strength Origins from OpenPowerlifting. Overall (all bodyweights) men.
sources.unit_as_published: lb with kg equivalents (kg shown here)
sources.notes: n is unique male lifters. Page says it holds all 99 percentile values but displays only 10th to 90th; no p95/p99 shown. Not independent of van den Hoek 2024 or Fitness Volt (same OpenPowerlifting source). The Stronger app page (strongermobileapp.com/standards/bench-press), also OpenPowerlifting-derived, gives an all-bodyweight male median of 127 kg from 1,668,369 results / 556,880 lifters (tested men 125 kg vs untested 138 kg) but no upper percentiles.

definition: Best successful competition bench press divided by the lifter's bodyweight at that competition (ratio), from drug-tested, unequipped (raw) powerlifting meets in 15 federations worldwide, 1968-2022, lifters aged 12+; athletes can appear more than once. Deciles for males aged 18-35 (UN young adult band), N = 306,061 bench press entries. Also stratified by IPF weight class (Table 6) and by other age bands (Table 4).
caveat: No source publishes a 99th percentile for men's bench press across all bodyweights. The best peer-reviewed source (van den Hoek 2024) stops at the 90th decile and reports strength as a multiple of bodyweight, not kg; its 18-35 male p90 is 1.96x bodyweight. Strength Level gives kg but its top published level is the 95th percentile (160 kg for men overall, 2015-2026 self-reported app lifts). The only p99 figures (Fitness Volt, OpenPowerlifting-derived) exist per weight class only: 187.5 kg at 83 kg, 200 kg at 93 kg, 215 kg at 105 kg. Every competition-based source (van den Hoek, Fitness Volt, Strength Origins, Stronger) draws on the same OpenPowerlifting database and describes competitive powerlifters, a far stronger group than men in general; the Cooper Institute norms are closer to a general tested population but top out at the 95th percentile and are bodyweight ratios of uncertain vintage (2007 edition). The question asks about 'men' without qualification; all answers here are gated by either competing in powerlifting or logging lifts in an app.

new_metric.label: Bench press one-rep max
new_metric.definition: Heaviest weight a person can bench press for a single repetition, in kilograms; competition sources use the best successful raw (unequipped) lift at a sanctioned powerlifting meet, app sources use an estimated one-rep max from logged sets.
phrasings: how much can the top 1% of men bench press
how much should i be able to bench press
